subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5! In this unit you will become confident with the angle rules that geometry is built on, and you will learn to construct accurate figures using a ruler, a protractor and a pair of compasses. Angles are all around you. When Amina watches the hands of the masjid clock move from Dhuhr towards Asr, when Yusuf works out the slope of a roof in Hargeisa, or when Hassan plans where two roads should meet in Mogadishu, they are all working with angles whether they name them or not.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use the fact that angles around a point sum to 360° to find unknown angles.
Use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° to find unknown angles.
Identify and use vertically opposite angles, which are always equal.
Use the rule that the angles in a triangle sum to 180°.
Identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines, and use their relationships.
Measure and draw angles accurately with a protractor, to the nearest degree.
Use a ruler and compasses to bisect a line segment, bisect an angle, and drop a perpendicular.
Construct triangles and quadrilaterals from given measurements.
Solve multi-step problems that combine several angle rules, and give a reason for every step.

concepts.title: Angles on a Line and Around a Point
concepts.explanation:
Two rules are the foundation of everything in this unit, so learn them until they are automatic.

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. A straight line represents a half turn. If several angles sit along one side of a straight line and together make that half turn, their measures must add to exactly 180°. For example, if one angle on a line is 125°, the angle beside it must be 180° − 125° = 55°. Two angles that add to 180° are called supplementary.

Angles around a point sum to 360°. Imagine standing at a point and turning all the way around until you face your starting direction again – that is a full turn, and it measures 360°. If several angles share a common vertex and together fill the whole turn, they must add to 360°. This is true no matter how many angles there are: two angles of 180°, four angles of 90°, or any other combination, will always total 360°.

Consider a point O with four angles around it measuring 85°, 120°, 95° and 60°. Check: 85° + 120° + 95° + 60° = 360°. They fill the turn exactly, with no gap and no overlap. When you know every angle but one, you find the missing angle by subtracting the known ones from 360°. If three angles around a point are 75°, 140° and 85°, the fourth is 360° − (75° + 140° + 85°) = 360° − 300° = 60°.

These rules appear everywhere in real life. When several roads meet at a roundabout in Nairobi, the angles between neighbouring roads add to 360°. When Khadija cuts a round anjero into pieces, the angles of all the slices add to 360°. When the hands of a clock point in different directions, the angles they make around the centre add to 360°; at 3 o'clock the hands make a 90° angle, leaving 270° for the rest of the face.
concepts.example: A useful habit: after solving any problem of this kind, add your angles back up and check you get 180° for a line or 360° for a point. This simple check catches most mistakes before they cost you mark.

concepts.title: Intersecting Lines and Vertically Opposite Angles
concepts.explanation:
When two straight lines cross at a point, they make four angles. These four angles have a beautiful and useful pattern. The angles directly across the crossing point from each other are called vertically opposite angles, and they are always equal.

Let us see *why* they are equal, because in Year 7 a reason matters as much as an answer. Label the four angles a, b, c, d going around the crossing point. Angles a and b sit together on a straight line, so a + b = 180°. Angles b and c also sit together on a straight line, so b + c = 180°. Both expressions equal 180°, so a + b = b + c. Taking b away from both sides leaves a = c. In the same way, b = d. We have proved that vertically opposite angles are equal.

This is a powerful shortcut. If one angle where two lines cross is 65°, then the angle vertically opposite it is also 65° at once, with no calculation. The other two angles are each 180° − 65° = 115° (because they are on a straight line with the 65° angle). So the four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115° – notice they still add to 360° around the point, exactly as Concept 1 promised.

Two angles that sit next to each other along a straight line are called a linear pair, and a linear pair is always supplementary (adds to 180°). So when two lines cross, you have two facts working together: vertically opposite angles are equal, and adjacent angles form a linear pair that adds to 180°. Knowing just one of the four angles lets you find all four.

You can also work backwards using algebra, which is a favourite Year 7 skill. Suppose one angle is written as (3x + 15)° and the angle vertically opposite it is 75°. Because vertically opposite angles are equal, 3x + 15 = 75, so 3x = 60 and x = 20. Setting up an equation from a geometry rule and solving it is exactly the kind of reasoning that leads towards proof.
concepts.example: Real intersections show these rules at work. Where two straight roads cross in Kismaayo, the angle a driver turns through and the angle across from it are equal. When light reflects off a flat mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection – another example of equal angles created by crossing lines.

concepts.title: Angles in a Triangle
concepts.explanation:
Here is one of the most important facts in all of geometry: the three angles inside any triangle add up to 180°. It does not matter whether the triangle is small or large, thin or fat, tilted or upright – the interior angles always total exactly 180°.

Why is this true? Imagine a triangle drawn between three points. If you draw a line through the top vertex parallel to the base, the two ‘tilted’ angles of the triangle reappear beside the top angle as alternate angles (a rule you will meet in Concept 4). The three angles now lie together along the straight line through the top, and angles on a straight line add to 180°. So the three angles of the triangle must add to 180° too. This neat argument links triangles to parallel lines – geometry rewards you for connecting ideas.

This rule lets you find a missing angle whenever you know the other two. If a triangle has angles of 30° and 90°, the third angle is 180° − (30° + 90°) = 60°. A roof truss shaped like this – 30°, 60°, 90° – is common in building because the right angle makes it stable. If Farah measures two angles of a triangular garden plot as 48° and 72°, the third corner must be 180° − (48° + 72°) = 60°.
concepts.example: Some triangles have special names worth knowing. In an equilateral triangle all three sides are equal and all three angles are 60° (because 180° ÷ 3 = 60°). In an isosceles triangle two sides are equal and the two base angles (the angles opposite the equal sides) are also equal – a fact that turns many problems into quick calculations. If an isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40°, the two equal base angles share the remaining 140°, so each is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

concepts.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
concepts.explanation:
Parallel lines are lines that run in exactly the same direction and stay the same distance apart forever, so they never meet. On a diagram we mark them with matching little arrows. A transversal is a line that crosses two or more other lines. When a transversal cuts a pair of parallel lines, it creates eight angles, and these angles come in three special families.

Corresponding angles are equal. These are angles in the *same position* at each crossing – for example, both in the ‘top-right’ corner. On the page they form a shape like the letter F (which may be reversed or upside down). Because the two parallel lines point the same way, the angle patterns at each crossing are identical, so corresponding angles match exactly.

Alternate angles are equal. These lie on *opposite* sides of the transversal, between the two parallel lines. On the page they form a shape like the letter Z (which may be reversed). Alternate angles are equal whenever the lines are parallel, and they are the angles that make the triangle proof in Concept 3 work.

Co-interior angles are supplementary – they add to 180°. These lie on the *same* side of the transversal, between the parallel lines, forming a shape like the letter C or U. If one co-interior angle is 110°, the other is 180° − 110° = 70°. Co-interior angles are sometimes called ‘allied’ or ‘same-side interior’ angles.

These three families give you great flexibility. If you know just one of the eight angles, you can find all eight. Suppose the transversal makes an angle of 125° at the top line. The corresponding angle at the bottom line is also 125°; the alternate angle is 125°; and the co-interior angle is 180° − 125° = 55°. Each of the eight angles is therefore either 125° or 55°, and – as always – the four angles around each crossing add to 360°.

A word of care: these equalities only hold when the lines really are parallel. In fact the rule works in reverse too, which is very useful. If you find that corresponding angles are equal, or that alternate angles are equal, or that co-interior angles add to 180°, then the two lines must be parallel. This is how surveyors and builders check that two edges are truly parallel.
concepts.example: You meet these relationships every day. Railway tracks near Mombasa are parallel, and any road crossing them acts as a transversal. The parallel shelves in Omar's shop are crossed by an upright support, making equal corresponding angles. Recognising the F, Z and C shapes in a busy diagram is a skill that becomes fast with practice.

concepts.title: Drawing and Measuring with Ruler and Protractor
concepts.explanation:
Accurate drawing is a real mathematical skill, and it rewards patience. Your two everyday tools are the ruler (a straightedge for drawing and measuring straight lengths) and the protractor (a half-circle marked from 0° to 180° for measuring and drawing angles).

To measure an angle: place the small cross or hole at the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex of the angle. Turn the protractor so that one arm of the angle lies along the zero line. Now read the scale where the other arm crosses it. The protractor has two scales, an inner and an outer one; use the scale that starts at 0° on your chosen arm, and read off the number where the second arm points.

To draw an angle of a given size – say 65° – do the reverse. Draw one arm with your ruler and mark the vertex at one end. Place the protractor centre on the vertex with the arm along the zero line. Find 65° on the correct scale and make a small dot at the edge. Remove the protractor and use your ruler to draw a straight arm from the vertex through the dot. You have drawn a 65° angle.

Reading the right scale is where most mistakes happen. Before you read, decide whether your angle is acute (less than 90°) or obtuse (more than 90°). If the angle clearly looks acute but your reading says 130°, you have read the wrong scale – the true answer is 180° − 130° = 50°. Checking ‘does my reading match the type of angle I see?’ saves you from this common slip.
concepts.example: To construct a triangle from measurements you combine both tools. Suppose you must draw a triangle with a base of 8 cm and base angles of 50° and 60°. First rule the base 8 cm long. At the left end, measure and draw a 50° angle; at the right end, measure and draw a 60° angle. Extend both new arms until they meet – that meeting point is the third vertex, and your triangle is complete. Because you were given two angles and the side between them, only one triangle is possible, so everyone who follows the steps carefully gets the same shape.

concepts.title: Constructions with Compasses
concepts.explanation:
A pair of compasses draws circles and arcs of an exact radius, and with a ruler it can build precise figures without measuring any angles. These classical constructions, invented by ancient Greek mathematicians, show the logical power of geometry. The golden rule is: do not change the compass width in the middle of a construction unless the instructions tell you to.

Perpendicular bisector of a line segment. To cut a segment AB exactly in half at a right angle: open the compasses to more than half the length of AB. Put the point on A and draw an arc above and below the segment. Without changing the width, put the point on B and draw two more arcs, crossing the first two. Rule a straight line through the two crossing points. That line is the perpendicular bisector – it passes through the midpoint of AB and meets it at 90°. Every point on it is the same distance from A as from B.

Bisecting an angle. To cut an angle exactly in half: put the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc that crosses both arms of the angle. Move the point to where the arc crosses one arm and draw a small arc inside the angle; without changing the width, do the same from where the arc crosses the other arm, so the two small arcs cross. Rule a line from the vertex through that crossing point. This line is the angle bisector, splitting the angle into two equal halves.

Dropping a perpendicular from a point to a line. Put the compass point on the given point and draw an arc that crosses the line at two places. From each of those two places, draw arcs on the far side of the line so they cross. Rule a line from your original point through that crossing point; it meets the line at a right angle.
concepts.example: These three constructions are the building blocks for many others. You can combine an angle bisector with a perpendicular to make a 45° angle (bisect a right angle). You can use a perpendicular bisector to find the exact centre of a line. Precision matters here: keep your pencil sharp, press the compass point firmly so it does not slip, and draw arcs that are long enough to cross clearly.

methods.title: How to measure an angle with a protractor
methods.example: An angle is drawn on your page. Measure it accurately with a protractor, reading the correct scale, to the nearest degree.
steps: Put the protractor centre on the vertex.
Line up one arm with the zero line.
Decide if the angle is acute or obtuse, then read the correct scale.
Read where the second arm crosses the scale.

methods.title: How to bisect a line segment (perpendicular bisector)
methods.example: Draw a line segment AB that is 8 cm long, then construct its perpendicular bisector using compasses and a ruler.
steps: Open the compasses to more than half the segment.
Draw arcs above and below from one end.
Keep the same width and draw arcs from the other end.
Rule a line through the two crossing points.

methods.title: How to bisect an angle
methods.example: Draw an angle of 70° and bisect it using compasses so it is split into two equal 35° angles.
steps: Put the compass point on the vertex; draw an arc across both arms.
From each crossing point, draw arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule a line from the vertex through that meeting point.

methods.title: How to solve a multi-step angle problem
methods.example: A triangle has an exterior angle of 130° at one vertex, formed by extending one side. The angle inside the triangle at another vertex is 55°. Find the third interior angle, giving a reason for each step.
steps: Mark every known angle on your diagram.
Find a rule that unlocks one more angle.
Write the new angle with its reason.
Repeat until you reach the answer, then check totals (180° or 360°).

methods.title: Isosceles triangle
methods.example: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40°. Find the two equal base angles.
steps: The two base angles are equal and share what is left after the top angle.
Each base angle = 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

methods.title: Parallel lines
methods.example: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 125°. Find its corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles.
steps: Corresponding angle = 125° (corresponding angles are equal).
Alternate angle = 125° (alternate angles are equal).
Co-interior angle = 180° − 125° = 55° (co-interior angles are supplementary).

workedExamples.title: Angle on a straight line
workedExamples.prompt: Two angles sit together on a straight line. One is 125°. Find the other.
workedExamples.solution: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Missing angle = 180° − 125° = 55°. Check: 125° + 55° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Angles around a point
workedExamples.prompt: Around a point O the angles are 90°, 110°, 85° and x°. Find x.

workedExamples.title: Vertically opposite angles
workedExamples.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 72°. Find all four angles.
workedExamples.solution: The vertically opposite angle is equal, so it is 72°. Each of the other two is on a straight line with the 72° angle, so each is 180° − 72° = 108°. The four angles are 72°, 108°, 72°, 108°. Check around the point: 72° + 108° + 72° + 108° = 360°. ✓

workedExamples.title: A missing triangle angle
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle has angles of 48° and 72°. Find the third angle.
workedExamples.solution: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°. Third angle = 180° − (48° + 72°) = 180° − 120° = 60°.

workedExamples.title: Isosceles triangle
workedExamples.prompt: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40°. Find the two equal base angles.
workedExamples.solution: The two base angles are equal and share what is left after the top angle. Remaining = 180° − 40° = 140°. Each base angle = 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

workedExamples.title: Parallel lines
workedExamples.prompt: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 125°. Find its corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles.
workedExamples.solution: Corresponding angle = 125° (corresponding angles are equal). Alternate angle = 125° (alternate angles are equal). Co-interior angle = 180° − 125° = 55° (co-interior angles are supplementary).

workedExamples.title: Angles with algebra
workedExamples.prompt: At a crossing, one angle is (3x + 15)° and the vertically opposite angle is 75°. Find x.
workedExamples.solution: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so 3x + 15 = 75. Then 3x = 60, so x = 20. (Check: 3 × 20 + 15 = 75. ✓)

workedExamples.title: Two rules together
workedExamples.prompt: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. A co-interior angle is (2x + 30)° and the other co-interior angle is (3x + 15)°. Find x and both angles.
workedExamples.solution: Co-interior angles are supplementary, so (2x + 30) + (3x + 15) = 180. That gives 5x + 45 = 180, so 5x = 135 and x = 27. The angles are 2(27) + 30 = 84° and 3(27) + 15 = 96°. Check: 84° + 96° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Straight line angles with algebra
workedExamples.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are (2x)° and (3x)°. Find x and both angles.
workedExamples.solution: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. 2x + 3x = 180 → 5x = 180 → x = 36. The angles are 2(36) = 72° and 3(36) = 108°. Check: 72° + 108° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Parallelogram angles
workedExamples.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle of 68°. Find the other three angles.
workedExamples.solution: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. The opposite angle = 68°. Each adjacent angle = 180° − 68° = 112°. The four angles are 68°, 112°, 68°, 112°.

workedExamples.title: Name the angle rule shown by each shape
workedExamples.prompt: Name the angle rule shown by each shape: a) an F-shape, b) a Z-shape, c) a C-shape between parallel lines.
workedExamples.solution: a) An F-shape shows corresponding angles, which are equal. b) A Z-shape shows alternate angles, which are equal. c) A C-shape shows co-interior angles, which are supplementary (add to 180°).

workedExamples.title: Vertically opposite angles with algebra
workedExamples.prompt: At a crossing, one angle is (4y − 10)° and its vertically opposite angle is (2y + 30)°. Find y and the angle.

activities.title: The Human Angle Clock
activities.materials: an open space and one other person (or your own two arms).
steps: Stand with both arms pointing straight up together – that is a 0° angle between them.
Slowly open one arm out. Stop and estimate the angle, then have a partner check it with a protractor drawn on paper.
Make a right angle (90°), a straight angle (180°), and a reflex angle (more than 180°).
Turn all the way around once and count: you have turned through 360°. Discuss why a full turn is 360°.
This gets the feeling of angle size into your body, so estimates on paper become much better.

activities.title: Straw Triangles Investigation
activities.materials: drinking straws (or thin sticks), scissors, and a protractor.
steps: Cut straws into three pieces and join them into a triangle.
Measure all three angles with your protractor and add them up.
Make three more triangles of very different shapes and measure each one's angles.
Record every total. What do you notice? (They should all be about 180° – small differences are measuring error.)
You have just discovered, with your own hands, that the angles in any triangle sum to 180°.

activities.title: Parallel Lines Angle Hunt
activities.materials: a ruler, a pencil, and coloured pencils.
steps: Draw two parallel lines (use the two long edges of your ruler to keep them equally apart).
Draw a slanting transversal across both lines.
Colour all the corresponding angles one colour, all the alternate angles a second colour, and the co-interior pairs a third.
Measure a few to confirm: corresponding and alternate are equal, co-interior add to 180°.

activities.title: Compass Construction Challenge
activities.materials: a pair of compasses, a ruler, a sharp pencil.
steps: Draw a line segment 10 cm long and construct its perpendicular bisector. Measure to check it cuts the segment at 5 cm and at 90°.
Draw any angle and bisect it with compasses. Measure both halves to check they are equal.
Combine your skills: construct a right angle, then bisect it to make a 45° angle.
Keep your best construction to show your teacher at your next session.

activities.title: Angle Rules Game (Family or Group)
activities.materials: paper cards and a family member, friend, or your AI tutor to play with (or play solo by timing yourself).
steps: On each card write an angle situation, e.g. ‘angles on a straight line, one is 130°’.
Shuffle the cards and take turns drawing one.
The player must state the rule and give the missing angle out loud within ten seconds.
A correct rule AND answer scores a point. First to ten points wins.
Playing alone? Time yourself stating the rule and answer out loud, and try to beat your best time each round.
Saying the rule out loud, not just the number, is what builds real geometry skill.

activities.title: Angles Around You (Real-World Investigation)
activities.materials: a protractor or a phone angle app, and a notebook.
steps: Walk around your home and find five angles: a door ajar, a roof slope, where two roads meet, an open book, a pair of scissors.
Estimate each angle first, then measure it. Record both numbers.
Sort your angles into acute, right, obtuse and reflex.
Find one place where two lines are parallel and something crosses them – describe the angles you see.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity made an angle rule finally click for you? Which construction was hardest to get accurate, and why? What would you like more practice with before the next teacher session? Share your answers at your next meeting.

rules.title: Basic Angle Rules
rules.text: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Angles around a point add to 360°. Vertically opposite angles (where two lines cross) are equal. The three angles in a triangle add to 180°. The four angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°.

rules.title: Parallel-Line Rules
rules.text: Corresponding angles (F-shape) are equal. Alternate angles (Z-shape) are equal. Co-interior angles (C-shape) are supplementary — they add to 180°. These rules only work when the lines are parallel.

rules.title: Angle Types
rules.text: Acute: less than 90°. Right: exactly 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: exactly 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°.

terms: The point where two lines or arms meet
Equal angles opposite where two lines cross
A line crossing two or more other lines
Equal angle pairs at parallel lines (F / Z)
Same-side angles at parallel lines; add to 180° (C)
commonMistakes: Around a point use 360°; on a line use 180°
Check the reading matches acute or obtuse
Always state the angle rule you used as a reason, e.g. "vertically opposite angles are equal".
Only use corresponding/alternate/co-interior angle rules when the lines are actually marked or stated as parallel.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: P + Q + 80 = 180 → P + Q = 100; since P = Q, each = 50°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are (3x + 10)° and (2x + 20)°. Find x and both angles.
Two straight roads cross. One angle is 40° more than the angle next to it on a straight line. Find all four angles.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Let the smaller angle = x, so the larger adjacent angle = x + 40. Since they lie on a straight line, x + (x + 40) = 180° → 2x + 40 = 180° → 2x = 140° → x = 70°. The four angles are 70°, 110°, 70°, 110° (vertically opposite pairs).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Constructions with Compasses.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A pair of compasses draws circles and arcs of an exact radius, and with a ruler it can build precise figures without measuring any angles. These classical constructions, invented by ancient Greek mathematicians, show the logical power of geometry. The golden rule is: do not change the compass width in the middle of a construction unless the instructions tell you to.

Perpendicular bisector of a line segment. To cut a segment AB exactly in half at a right angle: open the compasses to more than half the length of AB. Put the point on A and draw an arc above and below the segment. Without changing the width, put the point on B and draw two more arcs, crossing the first two. Rule a straight line through the two crossing points. That line is the perpendicular bisector – it passes through the midpoint of AB and meets it at 90°. Every point on it is the same distance from A as from B.

rounds.explanation: To bisect means to cut exactly in half, so the original angle is split into two equal angles.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Acute / Obtuse / Reflex
games.description: Practise acute / obtuse / reflex through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Acute / Obtuse / Reflex” mean?
choices: Equal angles opposite where two lines cross
A line crossing two or more other lines
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Acute / Obtuse / Reflex means Under 90° / 90°–180° / 180°–360°.

rounds.prompt: Two angles lie on a straight line. One is 118°. Find the other.
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. 180° − 118° = 62°.

rounds.prompt: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 72°. Find its corresponding angle.
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Corresponding angles formed where a transversal crosses parallel lines are equal, so the corresponding angle is also 72°.

rounds.prompt: To construct a triangle when you know the length of all three sides, which tools do you mainly use?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Set the compasses to each side length in turn and use the ruler for straight edges to construct a triangle from three given sides (SSS).

games.title: Unit Champion: Supplementary / Complementary
games.description: Practise supplementary / complementary through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Supplementary / Complementary” mean?
choices: Equal angles opposite where two lines cross
A line crossing two or more other lines
Equal angle pairs at parallel lines (F / Z)
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Supplementary / Complementary means Add to 180° / add to 90°.

rounds.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One of the angles formed is 47°. Find the angle vertically opposite it.
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angle opposite the 47° angle is also 47°.

rounds.prompt: Which piece of equipment is used to measure the size of an angle?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: A protractor is a half-circle scale marked from 0° to 180°, used to measure and draw angles.

rounds.prompt: Four angles meet at a point: 90°, 80°, 100° and y°. Find y.
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Angles around a point sum to 360°. y = 360° − 90° − 80° − 100° = 90°.

selfAssessment: I can use the fact that angles around a point sum to 360° to find unknown angles.
I can use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° to find unknown angles.
I can identify and use vertically opposite angles, which are always equal.
I can use the rule that the angles in a triangle sum to 180°.
I can identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines, and use their relationships.
I can measure and draw angles accurately with a protractor, to the nearest degree.
I can use a ruler and compasses to bisect a line segment, bisect an angle, and drop a perpendicular.
I can construct triangles and quadrilaterals from given measurements.
I can solve multi-step problems that combine several angle rules, giving a reason for every step.
